title: Invalidating a Code Snapshot Cache on the Thing That Should Invalidate It
summary:
A fintech ops lead in London pastes the same incident report into the diagnosis tool twice, three days apart. Same file, same line, same confidence score, same proposed fix — except the schema changed on Tuesday and the fix is now wrong. Nobody lied to the system. The system did exactly what it was built to do. That is the uncomfortable part.

Corporate AI 365 caches its root-cause analysis against a hash of three things: the issue text, a snapshot of the code, and the model version. Same hash, same answer, every time — that is what makes an approval gate defensible instead of a coin flip. But a cache is only as honest as the thing that is supposed to invalidate it, and in a system that never connects to a live database, one of those invalidators is a file someone has to remember to re-export.

The cache key is smaller than it feels

When an engineer in Berlin imagines the input to a diagnosis, they picture the whole repository and the whole database. The cache key doesn't see either. It sees the source tree as committed, and a scripted schema export — a dump of tables, columns, constraints, and views that your own developer generates and checks in or uploads. No connection string, no query against production, ever. That's the non-negotiable we design around.

The consequence is that the hash is a function of two artifacts that move at different speeds. Code changes on every push; the diagnosis engine sees that immediately because it reads the repository directly through your GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, or Azure DevOps connector. The schema export changes only when someone runs the export again. If a migration adds a column in staging and the team forgets to regenerate the scripted schema, the code snapshot looks fresh, the hash looks fresh, and the cached diagnosis is served with full confidence — pointing at a column that no longer means what the analysis thinks it means.

This is not a bug in the caching strategy. It is the honest cost of refusing to hold a live connection. We could make the schema "always fresh" by letting the AI query production directly — and we have deliberately not built that, because the moment an AI reasoning engine can read live rows, your security review stops being a conversation and becomes a liability audit. So the trade-off stands: reproducibility and a clean trust boundary, in exchange for a manual step that has to be someone's job.

Why the manual step is the real risk in a lean team

That trade-off is tolerable when there's a senior engineer who owns schema hygiene as a matter of habit. It is a real exposure when there isn't one. Across European SMEs and mid-market firms right now, a large share of teams — on the order of six in ten by some recent industry surveys — report they simply cannot find qualified developers to fill open roles. A Dublin logistics company or an Amsterdam retailer running production support with three generalists instead of a platform team isn't being negligent when the schema export goes stale for two sprints. There's no spare capacity to own that discipline full-time.

That matters because the cost of a wrong diagnosis is not symmetric. Enterprise downtime has been estimated by industry research at a median in the region of US$9,000 per minute for large organisations — and a diagnosis that confidently points at the wrong column doesn't just fail to fix the incident, it burns the first twenty minutes of the incident on the wrong hypothesis. In a lean team without a senior engineer to sanity-check the AI's output on sight, that twenty minutes is the whole difference between a contained incident and an escalated one.

What we actually invalidate on, and what we deliberately don't

Given that, the design answer isn't to pretend the schema is always current. It's to make staleness visible instead of silent:

  • The cache entry records the export timestamp alongside the hash, so a diagnosis can be shown next to "schema last scripted: 11 days ago" rather than presented as uniformly fresh.
  • Any manual schema re-export forces a new hash and a new diagnosis run — it is treated exactly like a code change, not a side artifact.
  • Where the AI needs to confirm a live fact — row counts, actual values, current index usage — it writes a read-only query for a developer to run by hand. The result comes back to a human, not to our cache, which keeps the live-data boundary intact even when the stakes are high.
  • We deliberately don't hash at the whole-repository level for large monorepos; the key is scoped to the files and schema objects actually implicated, so an unrelated commit elsewhere in the codebase doesn't force a re-diagnosis that produces nothing new — and, just as importantly, a relevant change doesn't get buried in repository-wide noise.

None of this makes the schema export automatic. It can't be, without the live connection we won't build. What it does is turn "the diagnosis was wrong" into "the diagnosis was wrong and here is exactly which input was stale and when it was last updated" — which is the difference between a system you can audit and one you have to take on faith. For a team in London, Berlin, Amsterdam, or Dublin running production support without a bench of senior engineers, that audit trail is the thing that lets a junior developer trust the output enough to act on it, and lets a manager explain the decision afterward without hand-waving.

title: Terraform Remote State at Enterprise Scale: Backends, Locking, Bootstrapping, and Team Workflows
summary:
When you are the only one running Terraform, local state is fine. The moment a second engineer runs apply, you are one race condition away from a broken environment. And when you are running dozens of environments across teams, the questions get harder: who creates the state bucket, how do you split state so one bad apply cannot take down everything, and how do you give a team of twenty engineers safe access without handing everyone the keys to production?

This post covers the full picture: choosing a backend, the bootstrapping problem nobody warns you about, state layout strategy, locking, surgery when things go wrong, and the team workflow that holds it together.

Why local state breaks

terraform.tfstate on your laptop is a single point of failure. It cannot be shared. It cannot be locked. If your laptop dies, your state dies with it. Worse, if two people apply at the same time, the last write wins and the loser’s changes vanish from state while still existing in the cloud. That gap between state and reality is called drift, and it is painful to fix.

Remote state solves three problems: shared access, locking, and durability. But setting it up raises a question most tutorials skip.

The bootstrapping problem

Here is the chicken-and-egg problem: Terraform needs a backend to store state, but the backend itself (an S3 bucket, a DynamoDB table, a storage account) is infrastructure. Who creates it?

You have three options, and only one of them is right for teams.

Option 1: ClickOps. Someone creates the bucket by hand in the console. This works exactly once. Then nobody remembers the settings, the bucket has no versioning, no encryption, no lifecycle policy, and six months later someone asks why state history only goes back two weeks.

Option 2: A separate bootstrap Terraform project with local state. This is the standard answer. You keep one tiny Terraform project whose only job is to create the backend infrastructure. Its state stays local (or in a second-level backend), because it has to exist before everything else.

Option 3: Terraform managing its own backend. Do not do this. A Terraform project cannot reliably create the bucket that holds its own state. The init sequence makes this circular and fragile.

Here is what a bootstrap project looks like on AWS:

# bootstrap/main.tf - run once per account, state stays local
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.5"
}

provider "aws" {
  region = "us-east-1"
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "tfstate" {
  bucket = "myorg-terraform-state-prod"
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_versioning" "tfstate" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.tfstate.id
  versioning_configuration {
    status = "Enabled"
  }
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration" "tfstate" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.tfstate.id
  rule {
    apply_server_side_encryption_by_default {
      sse_algorithm = "aws:kms"
    }
  }
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block" "tfstate" {
  bucket                  = aws_s3_bucket.tfstate.id
  block_public_acls       = true
  block_public_policy     = true
  ignore_public_acls      = true
  restrict_public_buckets = true
}

resource "aws_dynamodb_table" "tflocks" {
  name         = "terraform-state-locks"
  billing_mode = "PAY_PER_REQUEST"
  hash_key     = "LockID"

  attribute {
    name = "LockID"
    type = "S"
  }
}

Versioning matters more than people think. If a state file gets corrupted, versioning lets you roll back to the last good version. Without it, you are reconstructing state from terraform import, resource by resource, which is exactly as fun as it sounds.

Run this once per account. Commit it to git. Then every other project points at the backend it created.

Picking a backend

Every major cloud has a native backend. The pattern is the same everywhere: an object store for the state file plus a locking mechanism.

AWS (S3 + DynamoDB):

terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket         = "myorg-terraform-state-prod"
    key            = "network/terraform.tfstate"
    region         = "us-east-1"
    dynamodb_table = "terraform-state-locks"
    encrypt        = true
  }
}

Azure (Blob Storage):

terraform {
  backend "azurerm" {
    resource_group_name  = "tfstate-rg"
    storage_account_name = "tfstatestore"
    container_name       = "tfstate"
    key                  = "network.terraform.tfstate"
  }
}

Azure handles locking natively through blob leases. No separate lock table to manage. One less moving part, and one less thing to misconfigure.

GCP (GCS):

terraform {
  backend "gcs" {
    bucket = "myorg-terraform-state"
    prefix = "network"
  }
}

GCS locking is native as well.

State layout: one file per blast radius

Do not put your entire infrastructure in one state file. Split by environment and by component. A layout that works:

prod/
  network/terraform.tfstate
  compute/terraform.tfstate
  data/terraform.tfstate
  dns/terraform.tfstate
staging/
  network/terraform.tfstate
  compute/terraform.tfstate

Three reasons for this:

  1. Blast radius. If the network state gets corrupted, compute and data are untouched. A bad apply can only destroy what is in its state file.
  2. Speed. A plan against a 5,000-resource state file is slow. A plan against 200 resources is fast. Engineers stop running plan when it takes ten minutes. Then they apply blind.
  3. Access control. Not everyone needs access to every state file. The data team does not need write access to network state. Smaller state files map cleanly to IAM boundaries.

The tradeoff is cross-component references. When compute needs the VPC ID from network state, use terraform_remote_state data sources or, better, pass values through a shared outputs pattern. It adds a little friction. The blast radius protection is worth it.

State locking in practice

Locking is automatic once the backend supports it. When you run apply, Terraform acquires the lock. Anyone else who tries gets an error instead of corrupting your state.

Two rules I follow:

  1. Never use -lock=false in a shared workflow. It exists for emergencies, like a stuck lock after a crashed apply. If you use it, tell the team first.
  2. If a lock gets stuck, terraform force-unlock clears it. Check with the team before you do. Someone might actually be mid-apply, and force-unlocking under them recreates the exact race condition locking was built to prevent.

State surgery: when you need to move resources

Sometimes the layout needs to change. You split a monolith state into components, or you move a resource from one team’s state to another’s. Terraform has tools for this, and they all operate on state without touching real infrastructure.

Move a resource between modules or addresses:

terraform state mv 'aws_instance.web' 'module.compute.aws_instance.web'

This rewrites the state file. The EC2 instance keeps running. Nothing is destroyed. But get the address wrong and Terraform will plan to destroy the old address and create the new one. Always run terraform plan immediately after a state mv. If the plan shows creates or destroys, you got the address wrong. Fix it before anyone applies.

Pull state down, fix it, push it back:

terraform state pull > /tmp/state.json
# edit carefully
terraform state push /tmp/state.json

This is the escape hatch for corrupted state. It is also the fastest way to make things worse if you edit the JSON by hand without understanding the schema. Use it as a last resort, and keep a backup of the original pull.

Remove something from state without destroying it:

terraform state rm 'aws_s3_bucket.legacy'

The bucket keeps existing in AWS. Terraform just stops managing it. Useful when decommissioning Terraform management of a resource, or when handing a resource to another team’s state file (rm here, import there).

Migrating from local to remote state

If you already have local state and need to move it, the process is straightforward:

  1. Add the backend block to your configuration.
  2. Run terraform init. Terraform detects the migration and asks: "Do you want to copy existing state to the new backend?" Say yes.
  3. Verify with terraform plan. It should show no changes.
  4. Delete the local terraform.tfstate and the backup. Commit the backend config.

The init migration is one of the few genuinely smooth operations in Terraform. It just works.

Keep secrets out of hardcoded config

Do not hardcode bucket names or credentials in your backend block. Use partial backend configuration and pass values at init time:

terraform {
  backend "s3" {}
}

terraform init \
  -backend-config="bucket=myorg-terraform-state-prod" \
  -backend-config="key=network/terraform.tfstate" \
  -backend-config="region=us-east-1" \
  -backend-config="dynamodb_table=terraform-state-locks"

This keeps environment-specific values out of version control and lets the same code work across dev, staging, and prod. In CI/CD, these values come from pipeline variables, not from the repo.

State files contain secrets

This one catches people. Terraform state stores every attribute of every resource, including passwords, keys, and connection strings, in plain text. Treat your state bucket like a secrets store:

  • Enable encryption at rest (the encrypt = true above, or the KMS config in the bootstrap).
  • Restrict IAM access to the state bucket to the CI/CD role and break-glass admins only. Engineers get read access for planning, not write.
  • Never commit a state file to git. Add *.tfstate and *.tfstate.backup to .gitignore on day one.
  • Enable bucket versioning so a corrupted state can be rolled back.

If you are already using Vault or a secrets manager for application secrets, that does not cover Terraform state. State is a separate secrets surface. Treat it as one.

The team workflow

The setup that works for most teams:

  1. Engineers run terraform plan locally against the remote state. Plans are safe. They change nothing. Read access to state is enough.
  2. Pull requests include the plan output. Reviewers check what will change before it changes.
  3. Only CI/CD runs terraform apply, after the plan is approved. The pipeline uses a dedicated IAM role with write access to state.
  4. Applies run serially per state file. The lock enforces this mechanically, but the pipeline should also avoid queuing parallel applies to the same state.

Local plan, reviewed apply, locked state. That is the whole discipline. It scales from two engineers to two hundred without changing shape.

Pre-flight checklist

Before you call your remote state setup done:

  • [ ] Backend infrastructure created via a bootstrap project, not by hand
  • [ ] Versioning enabled on the state bucket
  • [ ] Encryption at rest enabled
  • [ ] Public access blocked on the state bucket
  • [ ] Locking configured and tested (run two applies, confirm the second waits or fails cleanly)
  • [ ] State split by environment and component, not one giant file
  • [ ] .gitignore covers *.tfstate and *.tfstate.backup
  • [ ] IAM: engineers read, CI/CD writes, break-glass admins only
  • [ ] Backend values passed via -backend-config, not hardcoded
  • [ ] Team knows the force-unlock procedure and when not to use it

Closing

Remote state is not exciting work. Nobody demos a backend block at a conference. But every production Terraform setup stands on it, and every Terraform horror story I have heard starts with someone skipping one of the items on that checklist.

Get the backend right, split your state by blast radius, lock everything, and keep secrets out of git. The rest of your Terraform practice gets easier from there.

Next week: reusable Terraform modules for API gateway provisioning across Azure and AWS, with versioned module registries and composition patterns that survive team growth.

  -backend-config="bucket=myorg-terraform-state-prod" \
  -backend-config="key=network/terraform.tfstate" \
  -backend-config="region=us-east-1" \
  -backend-config="dynamodb_table=terraform-state-locks"

This keeps environment-specific values out of version control and lets the same code work across dev, staging, and prod. In CI/CD, these values come from pipeline variables, not from the repo.

State files contain secrets

This one catches people. Terraform state stores every attribute of every resource, including passwords, keys, and connection strings, in plain text. Treat your state bucket like a secrets store:

  • Enable encryption at rest (the encrypt = true above, or the KMS config in the bootstrap).
  • Restrict IAM access to the state bucket to the CI/CD role and break-glass admins only. Engineers get read access for planning, not write.
  • Never commit a state file to git. Add *.tfstate and *.tfstate.backup to .gitignore on day one.
  • Enable bucket versioning so a corrupted state can be rolled back.

If you are already using Vault or a secrets manager for application secrets, that does not cover Terraform state. State is a separate secrets surface. Treat it as one.

The team workflow

The setup that works for most teams:

  1. Engineers run terraform plan locally against the remote state. Plans are safe. They change nothing. Read access to state is enough.
  2. Pull requests include the plan output. Reviewers check what will change before it changes.
  3. Only CI/CD runs terraform apply, after the plan is approved. The pipeline uses a dedicated IAM role with write access to state.
  4. Applies run serially per state file. The lock enforces this mechanically, but the pipeline should also avoid queuing parallel applies to the same state.

Local plan, reviewed apply, locked state. That is the whole discipline. It scales from two engineers to two hundred without changing shape.

Pre-flight checklist

Before you call your remote state setup done:

  • [ ] Backend infrastructure created via a bootstrap project, not by hand
  • [ ] Versioning enabled on the state bucket
  • [ ] Encryption at rest enabled
  • [ ] Public access blocked on the state bucket
  • [ ] Locking configured and tested (run two applies, confirm the second waits or fails cleanly)
  • [ ] State split by environment and component, not one giant file
  • [ ] .gitignore covers *.tfstate and *.tfstate.backup
  • [ ] IAM: engineers read, CI/CD writes, break-glass admins only
  • [ ] Backend values passed via -backend-config, not hardcoded
  • [ ] Team knows the force-unlock procedure and when not to use it

Closing

Remote state is not exciting work. Nobody demos a backend block at a conference. But every production Terraform setup stands on it, and every Terraform horror story I have heard starts with someone skipping one of the items on that checklist.

Get the backend right, split your state by blast radius, lock everything, and keep secrets out of git. The rest of your Terraform practice gets easier from there.

title: Mastering AI in QA: How to Evaluate Prompts and Build Reliable Test Workflows
summary:
Generative AI and Large Language Models (LLMs) are transforming how software engineering teams design, execute, and maintain test automation. From auto-generating Selenium and Playwright scripts to analyzing dense CI/CD execution logs, AI-driven assistants significantly reduce routine manual effort.

However, integrating LLMs into Quality Assurance introduces non-determinism. Unlike traditional code, prompts can produce subtle variations, hallucinated assertions, or context drift across model updates. To build enterprise-grade QA workflows, teams need systematic evaluation frameworks and modern test management infrastructure.

The Non-Deterministic Challenge: Evaluating AI Output

When using AI to generate test scenarios or parse bug reports, standard binary assertions (pass/fail) fall short. A prompt that generates a perfect Cypress test case today might miss crucial edge-case validations tomorrow if the model's temperature or system context shifts.

Applying structured ai prompt testing methods is essential for validating context windows, benchmarking prompt accuracy against fixed datasets, and preventing hallucinations in AI-generated test artifacts.

Key techniques for prompt validation in QA include:

  • Counterfactual Prompt Testing: Swapping specific parameters (such as environment variables or user roles) within prompts to verify output consistency.
  • Temperature & Top-P Tuning: Calibrating randomness parameters to ensure test case generation remains deterministic and reproducible.
  • Regression Testing for Prompts: Running continuous evaluation suites whenever underlying foundation models or system prompts are updated.

By establishing rigorous ai prompt testing methods, engineering teams can transition AI from a risky playground experiment into a dependable QA asset.

Unifying AI and Automated Test Management

To maximize the ROI of AI in testing, generated test scripts and validation results must not remain isolated in chat windows. They need to seamlessly sync with your primary CI/CD pipelines and test management hubs.

Modern QA environments demand full synchronization between manual test cases, automated frameworks, and AI outputs. Leveraging next-generation ai test management tools gives engineering leaders centralized visibility into test execution status, flaky test trends, and overall release readiness.

2. Autonomous Debugging with AI Agents

When nightly regression runs fail, engineers often spend hours parsing raw CLI reports and console logs. Deploying an autonomous ai agent for qa testing accelerates root-cause analysis by instantly grouping log stack traces, mapping failures to recent code commits, and suggesting precise code fixes.

Every automated script generated or optimized by AI must be validated directly within continuous integration pipelines. Triggering an automated feature test upon pull request creation guarantees that newly generated test logic doesn't introduce regressions into existing suites.

title: Zero-Downtime Kubernetes Deploys: Probes, Rolling Updates, and PodDisruptionBudgets
summary:
Kubernetes advertises rolling updates out of the box, yet many teams still see a burst of 502s on every deploy. The defaults are only part of the story: zero downtime needs correct probes, a sensible rollout strategy, graceful shutdown, and protection from voluntary disruptions like node drains. This post walks through each piece with manifests you can apply today.

Why requests get dropped

During a rollout, three things can go wrong:

  1. New pods receive traffic before they are ready. The container process is running, but caches, DB pools, or JIT warm-up are not done.
  2. Old pods are killed while they still have in-flight requests. Endpoint removal and SIGTERM happen concurrently, so a pod may receive new connections after it starts shutting down.
  3. Too many pods disappear at once. A rollout combined with a node drain or autoscaler scale-down can drop capacity below what your traffic needs.

Each problem has a dedicated Kubernetes feature.

Step 1: Readiness, liveness, and startup probes

  • Readiness decides whether a pod is in the Service's endpoints. Fail it and traffic stops; the pod is not restarted.
  • Liveness decides whether the container should be restarted. Use it only for "this process is wedged" conditions.
  • Startup holds off liveness checks until a slow-starting app has booted. 
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
  labels:
    app: web
spec:
  replicas: 4
  revisionHistoryLimit: 5
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 25%
      maxUnavailable: 0
  minReadySeconds: 10
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: ghcr.io/example/web:1.4.2
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: 8080
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 250m
              memory: 256Mi
            limits:
              memory: 512Mi
          startupProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 5
            failureThreshold: 24   # up to 120s to boot
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /ready
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 5
            timeoutSeconds: 2
            failureThreshold: 2
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 10
            timeoutSeconds: 2
            failureThreshold: 3
          lifecycle:
            preStop:
              exec:
                command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 10"]

Keep /healthz cheap and local: it should answer "is my process alive?", not "is the database up?". If liveness checks a shared dependency, a database blip restarts every pod at once. /ready can check dependencies the pod truly can't serve without.

Step 2: A rollout strategy that never reduces capacity

The two knobs that matter:

  • maxUnavailable: 0 means Kubernetes never removes an old pod until a new one is Ready.
  • maxSurge: 25% lets it create extra pods (here, 1 of 4) above the desired count during the rollout.

minReadySeconds: 10 requires a new pod to stay Ready for 10 seconds before it counts as available. That catches apps that pass their first readiness check and then crash.

The trade-off is that you need spare cluster capacity for the surge pods. If your cluster is tightly packed, the rollout stalls in Pending instead of dropping traffic, which is the failure mode you want.

Step 3: Graceful shutdown

When a pod is deleted, Kubernetes sends SIGTERM and, in parallel, removes the pod from Service endpoints. kube-proxy, ingress controllers, and cloud load balancers take a few seconds to notice. The preStop sleep above keeps the pod serving during that window; only then does SIGTERM reach your process.

Your application must also handle SIGTERM by finishing in-flight requests. A minimal Python example:

import signal
import sys
from http.server import ThreadingHTTPServer, BaseHTTPRequestHandler
import threading


class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        body = b"ok"
        self.send_response(200)
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(body)))
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(body)


server = ThreadingHTTPServer(("0.0.0.0", 8080), Handler)


def shutdown(signum, frame):
    # shutdown() blocks until serve_forever exits, so run it in a thread
    threading.Thread(target=server.shutdown, daemon=True).start()


signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, shutdown)
server.serve_forever()
server.server_close()
sys.exit(0)

Make sure terminationGracePeriodSeconds exceeds the preStop sleep plus your longest request. Otherwise the kubelet sends SIGKILL mid-request.

Step 4: PodDisruptionBudgets for voluntary disruptions

Rollouts aren't the only time pods go away. kubectl drain, cluster upgrades, and the cluster autoscaler all evict pods. A PodDisruptionBudget (PDB) tells the eviction API how many pods must stay up:

apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: web-pdb
spec:
  minAvailable: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web

With 4 replicas and minAvailable: 3, a drain evicts at most one web pod at a time and waits for its replacement to become Ready. Spread the replicas across nodes so a single drain doesn't touch most of them:

      topologySpreadConstraints:
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
          whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
          labelSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: web

(Add that under spec.template.spec in the Deployment.)

Step 5: Deploy and verify with kubectl 

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

NS="${NS:-default}"
IMAGE="${1:?usage: deploy.sh }"

kubectl -n "$NS" set image deployment/web web="$IMAGE"
kubectl -n "$NS" annotate deployment/web \
  kubernetes.io/change-cause="deploy $IMAGE" --overwrite

if ! kubectl -n "$NS" rollout status deployment/web --timeout=300s; then
  echo "Rollout failed, rolling back" >&2
  kubectl -n "$NS" rollout undo deployment/web
  kubectl -n "$NS" rollout status deployment/web --timeout=300s
  exit 1
fi

kubectl -n "$NS" get pdb web-pdb

Set spec.progressDeadlineSeconds (default 600) so a stuck rollout is reported as failed and rollout status exits non-zero.

To prove zero downtime, run a load loop against the Service while deploying:

while true; do
  code=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://web.default.svc.cluster.local/)
  [ "$code" != "200" ] && echo "$(date +%T) got $code"
  sleep 0.1
done

Any line printed during a rollout is a dropped request worth investigating.

Common pitfalls

  • Liveness probe identical to readiness, checking the database. One dependency outage becomes a cluster-wide restart storm.
  • No preStop delay. Traffic still routes to terminating pods for a few seconds, causing connection resets.
  • minAvailable equal to replicas. The PDB blocks every drain forever, and node upgrades hang.
  • Single replica. No probe or PDB can make one pod zero-downtime. Run at least two.
  • Shells that swallow signals. command: ["sh", "-c", "python app.py"] may leave sh as PID 1, and it won't forward SIGTERM. Use exec or an init like tini.
  • Probe timeouts too tight. A 1s timeout on a GC-heavy JVM causes flapping under load.

Wrap-up

Zero-downtime deploys come from layers that work together: probes gate traffic, maxUnavailable: 0 preserves capacity, preStop plus SIGTERM handling drains connections, and PDBs guard against drains. Add the curl loop to your staging pipeline and you'll catch regressions before users do.

title: Unlocking Android Power: A Deep Dive into Termux for Mobile Development
summary:
Introduction

Termux is a terminal emulator and Linux environment that runs on Android without rooting. It gives you access to a powerful package manager (pkg), a full Bash shell, and a curated collection of Linux tools—all from your phone or tablet. For developers, Termux turns a mobile device into a portable dev workstation: you can write scripts, run Python or Node.js, compile C programs, manage Git repos, and even SSH into remote servers.

Getting Started

Installation

  1. Open the Google Play Store or F-Droid and install the Termux app.
  2. Launch Termux. The first run will populate the $HOME directory and set up the default package repositories.
  3. Update the package index: 
apt update && apt upgrade -y

Tip: Use apt or its wrapper pkg interchangeably; pkg adds colour and shortcuts.

Core Package Management

Termux uses the same apt backend as Debian/Ubuntu, but packages are compiled for Android's ARM or x86_64 architectures.

Installing Common Tools 

pkg install git python nodejs curl wget neovim tmux openssh
  • git – version control
  • python – scripting and data work
  • nodejs – JavaScript runtime
  • neovim – lightweight editor
  • tmux – terminal multiplexer for persistent sessions
  • openssh – SSH client/server

Searching and Removing 

pkg search 
pkg uninstall

All packages live under $PREFIX, which resolves to /data/data/com.termux/files/usr.

Writing Your First Script

Create a file called hello.sh:

echo "#!/data/data/com.termux/files/usr/bin/bash" > hello.sh
chmod +x hello.sh
cat >> hello.sh <<'EOF'
echo "Hello from Termux!"
EOF
./hello.sh

The shebang points to the Bash binary inside Termux, ensuring the script runs regardless of the Android shell.

Python Development

Termux’s Python package ships with pip. Install a virtual environment to keep dependencies tidy:

pip install --upgrade pip setuptools wheel
pip install virtualenv
virtualenv venv
source venv/bin/activate
pip install requests beautifulsoup4

Now you can write a quick scraper:

cat > scraper.py <<'PY'
import requests, bs4, sys
url = sys.argv[1]
resp = requests.get(url)
soup = bs4.BeautifulSoup(resp.text, 'html.parser')
print(soup.title.string)
PY
python scraper.py https://dev.to

All of this runs on a phone with the same speed you’d expect from a low‑end laptop.

Node.js and npm

Node.js works out of the box. Install a project globally or locally:

npm init -y
npm install express
cat > index.js <<'JS'
const express = require('express');
const app = express();
app.get('/', (req, res) => res.send('Hello from Termux!'));
app.listen(3000, () => console.log('Listening on 3000'));
JS
node index.js &

You can reach the server from the same device via http://127.0.0.1:3000 or from another device on the same Wi‑Fi network using the phone’s IP address.

Using SSH

As a Client 

ssh user@remote-host.com

The first time you connect, accept the host key and you’re in.

As a Server 

apt install openssh
passwd   # set a password for the Termux user
sshd

Find your device’s IP with ip addr show wlan0. Then from a laptop:

ssh $(whoami)@

You now have a full remote shell on your Android device.

Persistent Sessions with tmux

tmux lets you detach from a session and re‑attach later, perfect for long builds or monitoring logs.

tmux new -s dev
# work inside the session
Ctrl‑b d   # detach
tmux attach -t dev   # re‑attach

title: Detecting Inbound Dead Air: Answered Calls Where Asterisk Never Accepts Carrier RTP
summary:
Detecting Inbound Dead Air: Answered Calls Where Asterisk Never Accepts Carrier RTP

Some inbound calls answer normally at the SIP level, but the PBX never accepts a single RTP packet from the carrier. Asterisk already logs the evidence: a Strict RTP "learning" line that never turns into a lock or a source switch. Here's how I turned that into an alert, corroborated it with Homer RTCP, avoided the early-media trap, and used one SIP header to decide where to send the ticket.

Tested on: Asterisk 18 (ViciDial build, chan_sip, strictrtp=seqno, ConfBridge/softmix agent bridges), Loki, Homer with heplify-server on PostgreSQL 16. Check your Asterisk version's res_rtp_asterisk.c for the exact log wording.

What does inbound dead air look like?

The agent answers and hears nothing. SIP looks normal (INVITE, 183, 200 OK, ACK, BYE), the CDR shows a short answered call, and the agent gets blamed. The first one I caught sat in the agent's bridge for about 6 seconds. Asterisk's log showed the carrier's media address set from SDP, then nothing: no packet from that stream was ever accepted.

Then it stopped being a one-off. One morning, 26 answered inbound calls in 44 minutes had no carrier RTP accepted at the PBX, across three inbound trunks: 26 of the 125 calls on those trunks that reached an agent bridge, about one in five. The previous day's 12 business hours had 1,330 bridged calls on the same trunks and none like this. What this shows is that no carrier RTP was accepted at the PBX; assigning blame needs packet captures or carrier evidence.

Which Asterisk log lines show whether RTP arrived?

With strict RTP enabled (strictrtp=yes, the default, or seqno), res_rtp_asterisk.c logs the source-learning state of every RTP stream at verbose level 4. Real lines from my server, with addresses, IDs and dates replaced:

[15:33:36] VERBOSE[17871][C-0001a2b3] res_rtp_asterisk.c: 0x7f7f... -- Strict RTP learning after remote address set to: 198.51.100.23:45892
[13:42:40] VERBOSE[3563][C-0001a0f0] res_rtp_asterisk.c: 0x7f7e... -- Strict RTP learning complete - Locking on source address 203.0.113.10:10256
[13:43:01] VERBOSE[6158][C-0001a0f3] res_rtp_asterisk.c: 0x7f7f... -- Strict RTP switching to RTP target address 203.0.113.20:30818 as source
[13:43:01] VERBOSE[6158][C-0001a0f3] res_rtp_asterisk.c: 0x7f7e... -- Strict RTP switching source address to 192.0.2.108:41882

What matters is where in the source each one is printed (Asterisk 18):

  • "learning after remote address set to" comes from ast_rtp_remote_address_set(). It fires when the far end's address is set from SDP. No packet is involved. Call it the open.
  • "Locking on source address", "switching to RTP target address ... as source" and "switching source address to" are all printed in ast_rtp_read(), the incoming-packet path. Each one means a packet arrived and Asterisk accepted that source. Call any of them a close.

A missing close doesn't mean zero packets hit the NIC. Strict RTP silently drops packets (debug level only) while it qualifies a different source address, which takes 4 sequential packets by default. So an open with no close means Asterisk never accepted a stream for that call. A real 50-packet-per-second stream bridged for several seconds should get through probation from any address, so an unpaired open is a strong candidate, but only a candidate.

Also, SDP says where the carrier wants to receive media, not where it sends from. A different source shows up as "switching source address to ", so the code pairs any close of the same stream within the carrier's ranges. A source outside your map becomes a false candidate that RTCP refutes.

Prerequisites: messages must log verbose at level 4 or higher, and you must match all three close forms. Over about four months my messages file had 414,530 opens, 369,649 "Locking", 234,563 "switching to RTP target" and 101,985 "switching source address" lines. Match only "Locking" and you'll flag healthy calls.

How do I tell an answered inbound call from a ring that went nowhere?

Unanswered calls also leave unpaired opens, since many carriers send nothing before the answer: 16 of 42 in a two-hour window around the incident. So for each unpaired open, read the lines with the same C- ID and check:

  • Bridge evidence. In my ViciDial build the customer channel goes into a ConfBridge softmix conference: Channel SIP/-xxxx joined 'softmix' base-bridge. Ring-group overflow via Dial() logs app_dial.c: SIP/... answered instead. The first such line is the join; left 'softmix' is the leave. MeetMe-based ViciDial setups log different lines.
  • Direction. The context must name the inbound trunk's channel and inbound dialplan context. With one peer name for both directions, a silent outbound leg looks identical at the RTP layer.
  • DID and caller ID, for the alert. MixMonitor and my dialplan's Phone call from ... line both run before the 200 OK, so neither proves an answer.

Here's the first incident, filtered to its C- ID:

15:33:36  Strict RTP learning after remote address set to: 198.51.100.23:45892
15:33:36  Executing [process@trunkinbound:10] Verbose("SIP/carrier_in-...", "Phone call from ...")
15:33:40  Executing [...] ConfBridge("SIP/carrier_in-...", "...,vici_agent_bridge,vici_customer_user")
15:33:40  Channel SIP/carrier_in-... joined 'softmix' base-bridge <...>
15:33:46  Channel SIP/carrier_in-... left 'softmix' base-bridge <...>

An open, a join, a leave six seconds later, no close.

This covers calls that reached a bridge. In the incident window one more call never locked: the PBX answered it into the queue and the carrier hung up 7 seconds later, before any agent. If queue dead air matters to you, anchor on the PBX's 200 OK instead.

How long should I wait for a close?

Don't measure the hold from the open, which happens when the call arrives: ring-group overflow calls ring a long time (48 s in a 12-hour sample).

Anchor on the join instead. From the raw log file over 12 business hours: 1,330 bridged inbound calls on the three trunks, every one closed, median close in the same second as the join, latest 2 s after it. These time the logged transition, not packet arrival, at one-second resolution. During the incident the latest healthy close was 5 s after the join.

My rule: no close for the call by join + 20 s. That's several times the worst case, and the candidate is ready well under a minute after the agent picks up.

What does the detector code look like?

My watcher reads the logs from Loki, but tailing messages works the same. This is the core matching logic, simplified from my production script with documentation-range addresses. It runs as shown:

import re

# One entry per inbound door. The SAME matcher is used for opens and closes.
CARRIERS = {
    "carrier_a":    {"media": (r"203\.0\.113\.\d+", r"198\.51\.100\.\d+"), "chan": "SIP/carrier_a_in_"},
    "carrier_b_nl": {"media": (r"192\.0\.2\.190",), "chan": "SIP/carrier_b_nl-"},
    "carrier_b_de": {"media": (r"192\.0\.2\.163",), "chan": "SIP/carrier_b_de-"},
}
for c in CARRIERS.values():
    c["re"] = re.compile(r"(?:%s):\d+" % "|".join(c["media"]))

# [C-call tag] ... res_rtp_asterisk.c: 0x -- Strict RTP 
RE_STRICT = re.compile(r"\[(C-[0-9a-f]+)\] res_rtp_asterisk\.c: (0x[0-9a-f]+) -- Strict RTP (.*)$")
RE_OPEN = re.compile(r"learning after remote address set to: (\S+)")
RE_CLOSE = re.compile(r"learning complete - Locking on source address (\S+)"
                      r"|switching to RTP target address (\S+) as source"
                      r"|switching source address to (\S+)")


def media_carrier(ip_port):
    for name, c in CARRIERS.items():
        if c["re"].fullmatch(ip_port or ""):
            return name
    return None


def parse_lines(lines):
    """lines: [(ts_ns, text)] for ONE PBX, complete for the window.
    Returns (opens, closes, multi).
    opens: the FIRST carrier-facing stream of each call (the inbound leg's).
    closes: {(call_tag, rtp_instance): [(ts_ns, seq)]}, carrier-range only.
    multi: call tags that opened more than one carrier-facing RTP instance
    (e.g. an overflow dialled out through a carrier). Flag those for review.
    seq is the position after a stable sort by time, so same-second lines
    keep their order."""
    ordered = sorted(enumerate(lines), key=lambda x: (x[1][0], x[0]))
    opens, closes, first, instances = [], {}, {}, {}
    for seq, (_, (ts, line)) in enumerate(ordered):
        m = RE_STRICT.search(line)
        if not m:
            continue
        cid, inst, event = m.groups()
        o = RE_OPEN.match(event)
        if o:
            if not media_carrier(o.group(1)):
                continue
            instances.setdefault(cid, set()).add(inst)
            if cid not in first:     # later re-opens (re-INVITE) and other legs: not covered
                first[cid] = {"ts_ns": ts, "seq": seq, "cid": cid, "inst": inst,
                              "ip_port": o.group(1), "trunk": media_carrier(o.group(1))}
                opens.append(first[cid])
            continue
        c = RE_CLOSE.match(event)
        if c:
            ip_port = next(g for g in c.groups() if g)
            # any address in a carrier range, so a learned source change pairs
            if media_carrier(ip_port):
                closes.setdefault((cid, inst), []).append((ts, seq))
    multi = {cid for cid, s in instances.items() if len(s) > 1}
    return opens, closes, multi


def first_close(closes, o, upto_ns):
    """First close of the SAME call and SAME RTP instance after the open and
    no later than upto_ns. Another call reusing the port, or another leg of
    this call, can't pair it."""
    for ts, seq in closes.get((o["cid"], o["inst"]), []):
        if (ts, seq) > (o["ts_ns"], o["seq"]) and ts <= upto_ns:
            return ts
    return None

Every Strict RTP line carries the call's C- tag and the RTP instance pointer (0x...), so closes are keyed by both, not by port. Carriers reuse ports, so a match keyed on port can let a later call's lock "close" a dead one. Keying on the instance stops another leg of the same call from closing it too, for example an overflow dialled back out through a carrier. Calls with more than one carrier-facing instance come back in multi, so you can review them; my two days of raw logs had none. Only carrier-range closes count, so a ring-group phone's stream doesn't. The input must be complete and in time order; the stable sort keeps same-second lines in file order.

A Loki query that feeds it:

{server="pbx", job="asterisk"} |= "Strict RTP" |~ "203\\.0\\.113\\.\\d+|198\\.51\\.100\\.\\d+|192\\.0\\.2\\.190|192\\.0\\.2\\.163"

LogQL literals use Go escaping, so a regex \. is written \\.. query_range returns newest-first by default and silently stops at limit, so use direction=forward, split any window that hits the limit until none does, and merge before parsing. Then check the pipeline against the source: for one 12-hour window, two Loki runs gave 2,121 and 2,016 opens where the raw messages file had 2,284. All numbers here come from the raw file.

Each pass keeps as a candidate any bridged inbound call with no close by join + 20 s plus an ingest margin, and sends it to Homer before posting.

Opens and closes must use the same matcher: an alias of mine that matched one carrier's two POP ranges for opens but one for closes made every healthy call on the other POP a false candidate.

What can Homer RTCP add?

Your own RTCP corroborates the log signal; it comes from the same reception state, so it isn't independent proof. The carrier's RTCP, where it sends any, is the closest thing to independent evidence short of packet captures at both ends.

Your side. In Asterisk 18 a report carries a reception block once the far end's SSRC is recorded (themssrc_valid), which happens after a packet passes strict RTP and then stays set. RFC 3550 only requires blocks for sources heard since the previous report, so another stack may drop the block between bursts; check yours. heplify stores RTCP as JSON in hep_proto_5_default. In 128,786 reports around the incident, report_blocks was a non-empty array or null, never empty, missing or unparseable, but the SQL below still treats those as unclear rather than "nothing received".

Here are my side's reports for one dead call, in seconds relative to the 200 OK:

T-0.6  {"sender_information":{"packets":250,...},"report_blocks":null}   <- before the answer
T+4.4  {"sender_information":{"packets":491,...},"report_blocks":null}
T+9.4  {"sender_information":{"packets":741,...},"report_blocks":null}
T+14.4 {"sender_information":{"packets":991,...},"report_blocks":null}

We sent 50 packets a second; no far-end SSRC was ever recorded.

The carrier's side. Under RFC 3550, a participant that has sent RTP since its last report sends a Sender Report; otherwise a Receiver Report. heplify's decoder only fills sender_information for a Sender Report, so a Receiver Report shows zeros. The stored type is useless here (on compound packets it's the last sub-packet, 202 on most of my rows), so I test for a non-zero NTP timestamp; in one hour of my data it always coincided with a non-zero packet count. In that dead call every carrier report had a zero NTP timestamp, and a report block for our stream with the sequence number climbing about 200 every 4 s.

Over one hour on that carrier's trunks, all 85 calls where our side reported reception got real Sender Reports from the carrier (1,680 of 1,723 carrier reports had a sender timestamp). The dead calls got Receiver Reports only. That corroborates the log signal: the carrier's RTCP stack didn't consider itself a sender at its SBC. Corroboration, not proof, and silent about further upstream. The other carrier's relay sent no RTCP my capture saw.

Why is RTCP from before the answer meaningless?

The first report above was emitted before the 200 OK. My PBX replies with 183 Session Progress with SDP and starts early media (ringback) at once, then sends the final 200 OK on answer. So it emits RTCP during the ring, when a healthy carrier usually isn't sending yet.

In the hour before the incident, all 148 bridged calls with my RTCP had our 183 before the 200 OK. 48 had a report before the answer, and all 48 pre-answer reports had no receiver block. From 2 s after the answer it flipped: 2,420 reports, all with a block, and no healthy call where they were all empty.

In the incident window a call torn down 3.7 s after the answer had one pre-answer report from my side, with no block. On RTCP alone it looks dead, but the Asterisk log shows it locked at the answer.

The rule I use:

  • Refuted: any report from your side, at any time, has a non-empty block. Asterisk accepted a packet. Don't post.
  • Confirmed: at least one report from your side 2 s or more after the 200 OK, and none of your reports for the call, read through the end of the call, has a block.
  • Unknown: no post-answer report yet (very short calls, capture lag). Re-check next pass, and say so if it never settles.

All 26 incident calls came back confirmed: 1 to 5 post-answer reports each from my side, read 20 minutes past the answer (so through the end of every call), none with a block, and no Sender Report from either carrier.

How do I find the right Homer dialog for a log line?

Homer doesn't know the C- ID, but the carrier's SDP has the media ip:port. It's one statement, so no result from a previous call can leak in. Run it with psql -v pbx_ip=... -v sig_ips=a,b -v media_ip=... -v media_port=... -v open_ts='YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS+00' -f. RTCP is joined to the dialog by sid, which only works if your heplify correlates RTCP to the SIP Call-ID (mine does; check a known call first). My raw columns are bytea; if yours are text, drop the convert_from(...) wrappers.

-- One statement, no carried-over variables. Inputs: pbx_ip, sig_ips (comma list),
-- media_ip, media_port, open_ts. Output: one row with a verdict.
WITH inv AS (   -- carrier INVITEs whose SDP carries the open's media endpoint
  SELECT i.sid,
         coalesce(substring(convert_from(i.raw,'UTF8') from '(?i)\nx-oid:\s*([^\r\n]+)'), '') AS x_oid
  FROM hep_proto_1_call i
  WHERE i.create_date BETWEEN :'open_ts'::timestamptz - interval '90 seconds'
                          AND :'open_ts'::timestamptz + interval '3 seconds'
    AND i.protocol_header->>'dstIp' = :'pbx_ip'
    AND i.protocol_header->>'srcIp' = ANY (string_to_array(:'sig_ips', ','))
    AND convert_from(i.raw,'UTF8') LIKE 'INVITE %'
    AND convert_from(i.raw,'UTF8') ~ ('\nc=IN IP4 ' || replace(:'media_ip', '.', '\.') || '\r?\n')
    AND convert_from(i.raw,'UTF8') ~ ('\nm=audio ' || :'media_port' || ' ')
), d AS (       -- exactly one dialog, or nothing
  SELECT min(sid) AS sid, min(x_oid) AS x_oid, count(DISTINCT sid) AS n FROM inv
), a AS (       -- first 200 to an INVITE, sent by the PBX
  SELECT d.*, (SELECT min(k.create_date) FROM hep_proto_1_call k
               WHERE d.n = 1 AND k.sid = d.sid
                 AND k.create_date BETWEEN :'open_ts'::timestamptz - interval '90 seconds'
                                       AND :'open_ts'::timestamptz + interval '10 minutes'
                 AND k.protocol_header->>'srcIp' = :'pbx_ip'
                 AND convert_from(k.raw,'UTF8') ~ '^SIP/2\.0 200 '
                 AND convert_from(k.raw,'UTF8') ~* '\ncseq:\s*[0-9]+\s+invite') AS t200
  FROM d
), r AS (       -- every RTCP report of that dialog, classified
  SELECT p.create_date, p.protocol_header->>'srcIp' AS src, x.j,
         CASE WHEN x.j IS NULL                                THEN 'unparsed'
              WHEN NOT x.j ? 'report_blocks'                  THEN 'missing'
              WHEN jsonb_typeof(x.j->'report_blocks') = 'null'  THEN 'none'
              WHEN jsonb_typeof(x.j->'report_blocks') <> 'array' THEN 'malformed'
              WHEN jsonb_array_length(x.j->'report_blocks') = 0 THEN 'empty'
              ELSE 'blocks' END AS rb
  FROM a
  JOIN hep_proto_5_default p
    ON p.sid = a.sid
   AND p.create_date BETWEEN a.t200 - interval '2 minutes' AND a.t200 + interval '20 minutes'
  CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT CASE WHEN convert_from(p.raw,'UTF8') IS JSON
                                  THEN convert_from(p.raw,'UTF8')::jsonb END AS j) x
  WHERE a.n = 1 AND a.t200 IS NOT NULL
), s AS (
  SELECT
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE rb IN ('unparsed','missing','malformed','empty')) AS unclear,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE src = :'pbx_ip' AND rb = 'blocks') AS pbx_with_block,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE src = :'pbx_ip' AND create_date >= (SELECT t200 FROM a) + interval '2 seconds') AS pbx_post,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE src = :'pbx_ip' AND rb = 'none'
                     AND create_date >= (SELECT t200 FROM a) + interval '2 seconds') AS pbx_post_none,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE src <> :'pbx_ip' AND jsonb_typeof(j->'sender_information') = 'object'
                     AND (j->'sender_information'->>'ntp_timestamp_sec') ~ '^[0-9]+$'
                     AND (j->'sender_information'->>'ntp_timestamp_sec')::numeric > 0) AS far_end_sr
  FROM r
)
SELECT a.n AS dialogs, a.t200, a.x_oid, s.*,
  CASE WHEN a.n <> 1 OR a.t200 IS NULL             THEN 'unknown'
       WHEN s.pbx_with_block > 0                    THEN 'refuted'
       WHEN s.unclear > 0 OR s.pbx_post = 0         THEN 'unknown'
       WHEN s.pbx_post_none = s.pbx_post            THEN 'confirmed'
       ELSE 'unknown' END AS verdict
FROM a, s;

The INVITE window allows 3 s of clock skew after the open. How did one SIP header point to a shared upstream?

The 26 calls came through three doors: 14 on Carrier A's direct trunk, 7 via Carrier B's NL-labelled SBC and 5 via its DE-labelled SBC. Three trunks failing in the same 44 minutes suggested something shared upstream.

The clue was in Carrier B's INVITEs, which carry an extra header:

INVITE sip:...                              (from Carrier B's SBC)
Call-ID: 
X-OID: 

INVITE sip:...                              (from Carrier A's direct trunk)
Call-ID:

Carrier B's own Call-IDs are UUIDs. The X-OID value has the same distinctive multi-field layout as Carrier A's Call-IDs on my direct trunk. It was on all 12 Carrier B dead calls, and that day on 651 of 651 inbound dialogs from the DE-labelled SBC and 346 of 349 from the NL-labelled one. The three without it showed one of our own extension or agent names in the From display name; I didn't dig further.

That doesn't prove Carrier A originated them. Shared SBC software could produce the same format, and simultaneous failures don't locate a fault. But it changed what I did: I widened the watcher, which had missed the 12 Carrier B calls, and put X-OID in every alert and ticket. Carrier B can confirm it against the upstream leg in its own signalling trace. Look at a full INVITE from each of your trunks for similar headers.

How do I keep the watcher from going silently blind?

A detector that finds nothing looks healthy. Each guard is a reason to investigate, not a diagnosis:

  • Empty is never clean. No strict-RTP lines? Check the PBX stream has any recent lines; warn after 24 hours without them.
  • Freshness. Newest PBX line older than 45 s? Skip the pass without advancing coverage. Tune it to your traffic.
  • Coverage per trunk. Hourly, for each trunk with 10+ inbound calls, count how many opened a stream on a mapped address. Below half means the media moved, the log format changed, or the classifier broke. One carrier's media move left my watcher blind until this check existed.
  • Keep Homer off the critical path. Short timeout, per-pass budget. A candidate still unsettled after 10 minutes is posted as "unconfirmed" only if bridged within 20 s of the open, in the bridge 5 s or more, and still unclosed.
  • Replay. A --dry-run mode with --start/--end runs the same rule over a past window and writes nothing. I replayed this version over the previous week before switching.

What doesn't this catch?

  • Silent RTP. Packets can flow with 0% loss and carry near-silence. For a complaint, check the recording's inbound leg.
  • Media that stops later. A stream that locks and then dies mid-call is out of scope. So is a re-INVITE whose new stream never locks.
  • Calls that never reach a bridge. See the queued call above.
  • Who hung up. Don't assume it was the caller giving up. In the 26 incident calls, the first BYE came from the PBX side on 15 and from the carrier on 11.

event_model_payload.summary:
Detecting Inbound Dead Air: Answered Calls Where Asterisk Never Accepts Carrier RTP

Some inbound calls answer normally at the SIP level, but the PBX never accepts a single RTP packet from the carrier. Asterisk already logs the evidence: a Strict RTP "learning" line that never turns into a lock or a source switch. Here's how I turned that into an alert, corroborated it with Homer RTCP, avoided the early-media trap, and used one SIP header to decide where to send the ticket.

Tested on: Asterisk 18 (ViciDial build, chan_sip, strictrtp=seqno, ConfBridge/softmix agent bridges), Loki, Homer with heplify-server on PostgreSQL 16. Check your Asterisk version's res_rtp_asterisk.c for the exact log wording.

What does inbound dead air look like?

The agent answers and hears nothing. SIP looks normal (INVITE, 183, 200 OK, ACK, BYE), the CDR shows a short answered call, and the agent gets blamed. The first one I caught sat in the agent's bridge for about 6 seconds. Asterisk's log showed the carrier's media address set from SDP, then nothing: no packet from that stream was ever accepted.

Then it stopped being a one-off. One morning, 26 answered inbound calls in 44 minutes had no carrier RTP accepted at the PBX, across three inbound trunks: 26 of the 125 calls on those trunks that reached an agent bridge, about one in five. The previous day's 12 business hours had 1,330 bridged calls on the same trunks and none like this. What this shows is that no carrier RTP was accepted at the PBX; assigning blame needs packet captures or carrier evidence.

Which Asterisk log lines show whether RTP arrived?

With strict RTP enabled (strictrtp=yes, the default, or seqno), res_rtp_asterisk.c logs the source-learning state of every RTP stream at verbose level 4. Real lines from my server, with addresses, IDs and dates replaced:

[15:33:36] VERBOSE[17871][C-0001a2b3] res_rtp_asterisk.c: 0x7f7f... -- Strict RTP learning after remote address set to: 198.51.100.23:45892
[13:42:40] VERBOSE[3563][C-0001a0f0] res_rtp_asterisk.c: 0x7f7e... -- Strict RTP learning complete - Locking on source address 203.0.113.10:10256
[13:43:01] VERBOSE[6158][C-0001a0f3] res_rtp_asterisk.c: 0x7f7f... -- Strict RTP switching to RTP target address 203.0.113.20:30818 as source
[13:43:01] VERBOSE[6158][C-0001a0f3] res_rtp_asterisk.c: 0x7f7e... -- Strict RTP switching source address to 192.0.2.108:41882

What matters is where in the source each one is printed (Asterisk 18):

  • "learning after remote address set to" comes from ast_rtp_remote_address_set(). It fires when the far end's address is set from SDP. No packet is involved. Call it the open.
  • "Locking on source address", "switching to RTP target address ... as source" and "switching source address to" are all printed in ast_rtp_read(), the incoming-packet path. Each one means a packet arrived and Asterisk accepted that source. Call any of them a close.

A missing close doesn't mean zero packets hit the NIC. Strict RTP silently drops packets (debug level only) while it qualifies a different source address, which takes 4 sequential packets by default. So an open with no close means Asterisk never accepted a stream for that call. A real 50-packet-per-second stream bridged for several seconds should get through probation from any address, so an unpaired open is a strong candidate, but only a candidate.

Also, SDP says where the carrier wants to receive media, not where it sends from. A different source shows up as "switching source address to ", so the code pairs any close of the same stream within the carrier's ranges. A source outside your map becomes a false candidate that RTCP refutes.

Prerequisites: messages must log verbose at level 4 or higher, and you must match all three close forms. Over about four months my messages file had 414,530 opens, 369,649 "Locking", 234,563 "switching to RTP target" and 101,985 "switching source address" lines. Match only "Locking" and you'll flag healthy calls.

How do I tell an answered inbound call from a ring that went nowhere?

Unanswered calls also leave unpaired opens, since many carriers send nothing before the answer: 16 of 42 in a two-hour window around the incident. So for each unpaired open, read the lines with the same C- ID and check:

  • Bridge evidence. In my ViciDial build the customer channel goes into a ConfBridge softmix conference: Channel SIP/-xxxx joined 'softmix' base-bridge. Ring-group overflow via Dial() logs app_dial.c: SIP/... answered instead. The first such line is the join; left 'softmix' is the leave. MeetMe-based ViciDial setups log different lines.
  • Direction. The context must name the inbound trunk's channel and inbound dialplan context. With one peer name for both directions, a silent outbound leg looks identical at the RTP layer.
  • DID and caller ID, for the alert. MixMonitor and my dialplan's Phone call from ... line both run before the 200 OK, so neither proves an answer.

Here's the first incident, filtered to its C- ID:

15:33:36  Strict RTP learning after remote address set to: 198.51.100.23:45892
15:33:36  Executing [process@trunkinbound:10] Verbose("SIP/carrier_in-...", "Phone call from ...")
15:33:40  Executing [...] ConfBridge("SIP/carrier_in-...", "...,vici_agent_bridge,vici_customer_user")
15:33:40  Channel SIP/carrier_in-... joined 'softmix' base-bridge <...>
15:33:46  Channel SIP/carrier_in-... left 'softmix' base-bridge <...>

An open, a join, a leave six seconds later, no close.

This covers calls that reached a bridge. In the incident window one more call never locked: the PBX answered it into the queue and the carrier hung up 7 seconds later, before any agent. If queue dead air matters to you, anchor on the PBX's 200 OK instead.

How long should I wait for a close?

Don't measure the hold from the open, which happens when the call arrives: ring-group overflow calls ring a long time (48 s in a 12-hour sample).

Anchor on the join instead. From the raw log file over 12 business hours: 1,330 bridged inbound calls on the three trunks, every one closed, median close in the same second as the join, latest 2 s after it. These time the logged transition, not packet arrival, at one-second resolution. During the incident the latest healthy close was 5 s after the join.

My rule: no close for the call by join + 20 s. That's several times the worst case, and the candidate is ready well under a minute after the agent picks up.

What does the detector code look like?

My watcher reads the logs from Loki, but tailing messages works the same. This is the core matching logic, simplified from my production script with documentation-range addresses. It runs as shown:

import re

# One entry per inbound door. The SAME matcher is used for opens and closes.
CARRIERS = {
    "carrier_a":    {"media": (r"203\.0\.113\.\d+", r"198\.51\.100\.\d+"), "chan": "SIP/carrier_a_in_"},
    "carrier_b_nl": {"media": (r"192\.0\.2\.190",), "chan": "SIP/carrier_b_nl-"},
    "carrier_b_de": {"media": (r"192\.0\.2\.163",), "chan": "SIP/carrier_b_de-"},
}
for c in CARRIERS.values():
    c["re"] = re.compile(r"(?:%s):\d+" % "|".join(c["media"]))

# [C-call tag] ... res_rtp_asterisk.c: 0x -- Strict RTP 
RE_STRICT = re.compile(r"\[(C-[0-9a-f]+)\] res_rtp_asterisk\.c: (0x[0-9a-f]+) -- Strict RTP (.*)$")
RE_OPEN = re.compile(r"learning after remote address set to: (\S+)")
RE_CLOSE = re.compile(r"learning complete - Locking on source address (\S+)"
                      r"|switching to RTP target address (\S+) as source"
                      r"|switching source address to (\S+)")


def media_carrier(ip_port):
    for name, c in CARRIERS.items():
        if c["re"].fullmatch(ip_port or ""):
            return name
    return None


def parse_lines(lines):
    """lines: [(ts_ns, text)] for ONE PBX, complete for the window.
    Returns (opens, closes, multi).
    opens: the FIRST carrier-facing stream of each call (the inbound leg's).
    closes: {(call_tag, rtp_instance): [(ts_ns, seq)]}, carrier-range only.
    multi: call tags that opened more than one carrier-facing RTP instance
    (e.g. an overflow dialled out through a carrier). Flag those for review.
    seq is the position after a stable sort by time, so same-second lines
    keep their order."""
    ordered = sorted(enumerate(lines), key=lambda x: (x[1][0], x[0]))
    opens, closes, first, instances = [], {}, {}, {}
    for seq, (_, (ts, line)) in enumerate(ordered):
        m = RE_STRICT.search(line)
        if not m:
            continue
        cid, inst, event = m.groups()
        o = RE_OPEN.match(event)
        if o:
            if not media_carrier(o.group(1)):
                continue
            instances.setdefault(cid, set()).add(inst)
            if cid not in first:     # later re-opens (re-INVITE) and other legs: not covered
                first[cid] = {"ts_ns": ts, "seq": seq, "cid": cid, "inst": inst,
                              "ip_port": o.group(1), "trunk": media_carrier(o.group(1))}
                opens.append(first[cid])
            continue
        c = RE_CLOSE.match(event)
        if c:
            ip_port = next(g for g in c.groups() if g)
            # any address in a carrier range, so a learned source change pairs
            if media_carrier(ip_port):
                closes.setdefault((cid, inst), []).append((ts, seq))
    multi = {cid for cid, s in instances.items() if len(s) > 1}
    return opens, closes, multi


def first_close(closes, o, upto_ns):
    """First close of the SAME call and SAME RTP instance after the open and
    no later than upto_ns. Another call reusing the port, or another leg of
    this call, can't pair it."""
    for ts, seq in closes.get((o["cid"], o["inst"]), []):
        if (ts, seq) > (o["ts_ns"], o["seq"]) and ts <= upto_ns:
            return ts
    return None

Every Strict RTP line carries the call's C- tag and the RTP instance pointer (0x...), so closes are keyed by both, not by port. Carriers reuse ports, so a match keyed on port can let a later call's lock "close" a dead one. Keying on the instance stops another leg of the same call from closing it too, for example an overflow dialled back out through a carrier. Calls with more than one carrier-facing instance come back in multi, so you can review them; my two days of raw logs had none. Only carrier-range closes count, so a ring-group phone's stream doesn't. The input must be complete and in time order; the stable sort keeps same-second lines in file order.

A Loki query that feeds it:

{server="pbx", job="asterisk"} |= "Strict RTP" |~ "203\\.0\\.113\\.\\d+|198\\.51\\.100\\.\\d+|192\\.0\\.2\\.190|192\\.0\\.2\\.163"

LogQL literals use Go escaping, so a regex \. is written \\.. query_range returns newest-first by default and silently stops at limit, so use direction=forward, split any window that hits the limit until none does, and merge before parsing. Then check the pipeline against the source: for one 12-hour window, two Loki runs gave 2,121 and 2,016 opens where the raw messages file had 2,284. All numbers here come from the raw file.

Each pass keeps as a candidate any bridged inbound call with no close by join + 20 s plus an ingest margin, and sends it to Homer before posting.

Opens and closes must use the same matcher: an alias of mine that matched one carrier's two POP ranges for opens but one for closes made every healthy call on the other POP a false candidate.

What can Homer RTCP add?

Your own RTCP corroborates the log signal; it comes from the same reception state, so it isn't independent proof. The carrier's RTCP, where it sends any, is the closest thing to independent evidence short of packet captures at both ends.

Your side. In Asterisk 18 a report carries a reception block once the far end's SSRC is recorded (themssrc_valid), which happens after a packet passes strict RTP and then stays set. RFC 3550 only requires blocks for sources heard since the previous report, so another stack may drop the block between bursts; check yours. heplify stores RTCP as JSON in hep_proto_5_default. In 128,786 reports around the incident, report_blocks was a non-empty array or null, never empty, missing or unparseable, but the SQL below still treats those as unclear rather than "nothing received".

Here are my side's reports for one dead call, in seconds relative to the 200 OK:

T-0.6  {"sender_information":{"packets":250,...},"report_blocks":null}   <- before the answer
T+4.4  {"sender_information":{"packets":491,...},"report_blocks":null}
T+9.4  {"sender_information":{"packets":741,...},"report_blocks":null}
T+14.4 {"sender_information":{"packets":991,...},"report_blocks":null}

We sent 50 packets a second; no far-end SSRC was ever recorded.

The carrier's side. Under RFC 3550, a participant that has sent RTP since its last report sends a Sender Report; otherwise a Receiver Report. heplify's decoder only fills sender_information for a Sender Report, so a Receiver Report shows zeros. The stored type is useless here (on compound packets it's the last sub-packet, 202 on most of my rows), so I test for a non-zero NTP timestamp; in one hour of my data it always coincided with a non-zero packet count. In that dead call every carrier report had a zero NTP timestamp, and a report block for our stream with the sequence number climbing about 200 every 4 s.

Over one hour on that carrier's trunks, all 85 calls where our side reported reception got real Sender Reports from the carrier (1,680 of 1,723 carrier reports had a sender timestamp). The dead calls got Receiver Reports only. That corroborates the log signal: the carrier's RTCP stack didn't consider itself a sender at its SBC. Corroboration, not proof, and silent about further upstream. The other carrier's relay sent no RTCP my capture saw.

The first report above was emitted before the 200 OK. My PBX replies with 183 Session Progress with SDP and starts early media (ringback) at once, then sends the final 200 OK on answer. So it emits RTCP during the ring, when a healthy carrier usually isn't sending yet.

In the incident window a call torn down 3.7 s after the answer had one pre-answer report from my side, with no block. On RTCP alone it looks dead, but the Asterisk log shows it locked at the answer.

The rule I use:

  • Refuted: any report from your side, at any time, has a non-empty block. Asterisk accepted a packet. Don't post.
  • Confirmed: at least one report from your side 2 s or more after the 200 OK, and none of your reports for the call, read through the end of the call, has a block.
  • Unknown: no post-answer report yet (very short calls, capture lag). Re-check next pass, and say so if it never settles.

All 26 incident calls came back confirmed: 1 to 5 post-answer reports each from my side, read 20 minutes past the answer (so through the end of every call), none with a block, and no Sender Report from either carrier.

How do I find the right Homer dialog for a log line?

Homer doesn't know the C- ID, but the carrier's SDP has the media ip:port. It's one statement, so no result from a previous call can leak in. RTCP is joined to the dialog by sid, which only works if your heplify correlates RTCP to the SIP Call-ID (mine does; check a known call first). My raw columns are bytea; if yours are text, drop the convert_from(...) wrappers.

-- One statement, no carried-over variables. Inputs: pbx_ip, sig_ips (comma list),
-- media_ip, media_port, open_ts. Output: one row with a verdict.
WITH inv AS (   -- carrier INVITEs whose SDP carries the open's media endpoint
  SELECT i.sid,
         coalesce(substring(convert_from(i.raw,'UTF8') from '(?i)\nx-oid:\s*([^\r\n]+)'), '') AS x_oid
  FROM hep_proto_1_call i
  WHERE i.create_date BETWEEN :'open_ts'::timestamptz - interval '90 seconds'
                          AND :'open_ts'::timestamptz + interval '3 seconds'
    AND i.protocol_header->>'dstIp' = :'pbx_ip'
    AND i.protocol_header->>'srcIp' = ANY (string_to_array(:'sig_ips', ','))
    AND convert_from(i.raw,'UTF8') LIKE 'INVITE %'
    AND convert_from(i.raw,'UTF8') ~ ('\nc=IN IP4 ' || replace(:'media_ip', '.', '\.') || '\r?\n')
    AND convert_from(i.raw,'UTF8') ~ ('\nm=audio ' || :'media_port' || ' ')
), d AS (       -- exactly one dialog, or nothing
  SELECT min(sid) AS sid, min(x_oid) AS x_oid, count(DISTINCT sid) AS n FROM inv
), a AS (       -- first 200 to an INVITE, sent by the PBX
  SELECT d.*, (SELECT min(k.create_date) FROM hep_proto_1_call k
               WHERE d.n = 1 AND k.sid = d.sid
                 AND k.create_date BETWEEN :'open_ts'::timestamptz - interval '90 seconds'
                                       AND :'open_ts'::timestamptz + interval '10 minutes'
                 AND k.protocol_header->>'srcIp' = :'pbx_ip'
                 AND convert_from(k.raw,'UTF8') ~ '^SIP/2\.0 200 '
                 AND convert_from(k.raw,'UTF8') ~* '\ncseq:\s*[0-9]+\s+invite') AS t200
  FROM d
), r AS (       -- every RTCP report of that dialog, classified
  SELECT p.create_date, p.protocol_header->>'srcIp' AS src, x.j,
         CASE WHEN x.j IS NULL                                THEN 'unparsed'
              WHEN NOT x.j ? 'report_blocks'                  THEN 'missing'
              WHEN jsonb_typeof(x.j->'report_blocks') = 'null'  THEN 'none'
              WHEN jsonb_typeof(x.j->'report_blocks') <> 'array' THEN 'malformed'
              WHEN jsonb_array_length(x.j->'report_blocks') = 0 THEN 'empty'
              ELSE 'blocks' END AS rb
  FROM a
  JOIN hep_proto_5_default p
    ON p.sid = a.sid
   AND p.create_date BETWEEN a.t200 - interval '2 minutes' AND a.t200 + interval '20 minutes'
  CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT CASE WHEN convert_from(p.raw,'UTF8') IS JSON
                                  THEN convert_from(p.raw,'UTF8')::jsonb END AS j) x
  WHERE a.n = 1 AND a.t200 IS NOT NULL
), s AS (
  SELECT
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE rb IN ('unparsed','missing','malformed','empty')) AS unclear,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE src = :'pbx_ip' AND rb = 'blocks') AS pbx_with_block,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE src = :'pbx_ip' AND create_date >= (SELECT t200 FROM a) + interval '2 seconds') AS pbx_post,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE src = :'pbx_ip' AND rb = 'none'
                     AND create_date >= (SELECT t200 FROM a) + interval '2 seconds') AS pbx_post_none,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE src <> :'pbx_ip' AND jsonb_typeof(j->'sender_information') = 'object'
                     AND (j->'sender_information'->>'ntp_timestamp_sec') ~ '^[0-9]+$'
                     AND (j->'sender_information'->>'ntp_timestamp_sec')::numeric > 0) AS far_end_sr
  FROM r
)
SELECT a.n AS dialogs, a.t200, a.x_oid, s.*,
  CASE WHEN a.n <> 1 OR a.t200 IS NULL             THEN 'unknown'
       WHEN s.pbx_with_block > 0                    THEN 'refuted'
       WHEN s.unclear > 0 OR s.pbx_post = 0         THEN 'unknown'
       WHEN s.pbx_post_none = s.pbx_post            THEN 'confirmed'
       ELSE 'unknown' END AS verdict

title: Your Docker Container Is Running… So Why Is Your Application Down?
summary:
A practical guide to debugging Docker containers like a real DevOps engineer.

Imagine this situation.

You deploy your application using Docker. Everything looks perfect.

docker ps

Output:

CONTAINER ID   IMAGE          STATUS
a1b2c3d4       my-app:latest  Up 10 minutes

Your container is running. Docker reports no problems. You feel confident.

Then someone messages you:

"Hey, the application is down. Can you fix it?"

You check the container again.

Still running.

You restart it.

Still broken.

You rebuild the image.

Still broken.

Welcome to the real world of DevOps. 😅

A running container does not necessarily mean a healthy application.

Let's learn how to troubleshoot Docker like an engineer instead of randomly restarting containers.

🧠 1. Understand the Difference Between Running and Healthy

Docker can tell you whether a container's main process is running. It cannot automatically guarantee that your application is working correctly.

For example, your container might be running while:

  • The application is listening on the wrong port.
  • A required environment variable is missing.
  • The application is responding too slowly.
  • A dependency has crashed.

Database:          UNREACHABLE ❌

docker logs -f my-app

docker logs --tail 100 my-app

Include timestamps:

docker logs -t my-app

Connection refused
Database connection failed
Address already in use
Permission denied
Missing environment variable

Sometimes the problem is not visible in the logs.

docker inspect my-app

Check its state:

docker inspect -f '{{.State.Status}}' my-app

Check its exit code:

docker inspect -f '{{.State.ExitCode}}' my-app

docker inspect -f '{{.State.Health.Status}}' my-app

  --name my-app \
  -p 8080:8080 \
  my-app:latest

-p HOST_PORT:CONTAINER_PORT

For example:

Your browser
     |
     v
localhost:8080
     |
     v
Docker host port 8080
     |
     v
Container port 8080
     |
     v
Application

my-app        95%       480MiB / 512MiB
database      15%       300MiB / 1GiB

docker ps -a
docker system df
docker events

Here's one way to improve your container monitoring.

  --start-period=10s \
  --retries=3 \

starting
healthy
unhealthy

docker network inspect my-network

If both services need to communicate, make sure they share an appropriate network.

With Docker Compose, services on the same default network can usually reach each other using their service names.

Example:

  app:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://app:password@db:5432/appdb
    depends_on:
      - db

  db:
    image: postgres:17
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: password
      POSTGRES_DB: appdb

Here, db is the database service name.

Important: This is a learning example, not a production-ready configuration. Use secrets rather than hardcoded passwords, persistent storage for database data, and application-level retry logic. Also, depends_on alone does not guarantee that PostgreSQL is ready to accept connections.
